apparent-wind.short: The wind a moving blade actually feels: the real wind combined with the headwind from the blade's own motion. Near the tips it is mostly the blade's own speed.

angle-of-attack.short: The angle between a blade's chord line and the air flowing past it. A few degrees gives strong lift; too many and the flow separates and the blade stalls.

aerodynamic-lift.short: The force on a wing or blade at right angles to the air flowing past it. On a wind turbine blade the lift points mostly downwind, but it leans slightly forward along the rotation, and that small forward part turns the rotor.

aerodynamic-stall.short: When the angle of attack gets too large, air peels away from the top of the blade: lift collapses and drag soars.

blade-pitch.short: Twisting a whole blade about its long axis. Turbines pitch their blades to catch the most power in light winds and to shed power in strong winds.

tip-speed-ratio.short: How fast the blade tips move compared with the wind. Large modern rotors run with their tips several times faster than the wind.

cut-in-speed.short: The wind speed at which a turbine starts producing power, typically about 3 m/s.

rated-wind-speed.short: The wind speed at which a turbine first reaches its full (rated) power. Above it the blades pitch to hold power steady.

cut-out-speed.short: The wind speed at which a turbine stops to protect itself, typically 25 m/s or more.

rayleigh-distribution.short: A simple bell-with-a-long-tail curve for how often each wind speed occurs at a site, set by one number: the mean wind speed.

induction-factor.short: How much a rotor slows the wind as it passes through, as a fraction of the free wind speed. The ideal rotor slows it by one third.

actuator-disc.short: An idealised rotor treated as a thin, permeable disc that takes energy from the flow. The simplest model that gives the Betz limit.

penstock.short: The large pipe that carries water from a reservoir's intake down to the turbines.

tailrace.short: The channel that carries water away from a turbine back to the river.

francis-turbine.short: A reaction turbine in which water spirals inward through a spinning runner whose curved blades are fixed in shape (not adjustable). The workhorse of medium- to high-head hydropower.

kaplan-turbine.short: A propeller-shaped reaction turbine with adjustable blades, suited to low heads and large flows.

pelton-turbine.short: An impulse turbine: jets of water hit a ring of split cups. Suited to very high heads and small flows.

run-of-river.short: A plant that uses a river's flow as it comes, with little or no reservoir, so its output follows the river.

flash-steam-plant.short: A geothermal plant that drops the pressure of very hot water from the well so part of it boils (flashes) into steam, which drives a turbine. Needs fluid above about 182 °C.

binary-cycle-plant.short: A geothermal plant in which hot brine heats a second fluid with a low boiling point; that fluid's vapour drives the turbine. Works with cooler resources.

dry-steam-plant.short: A geothermal plant fed directly by natural steam from the ground, the oldest kind (Larderello, The Geysers).

reinjection-well.short: A well that returns cooled geothermal water to the reservoir, keeping up pressure and disposing of the brine.

enhanced-geothermal-system.short: Man-made geothermal: fluid is pumped into hot, dry rock to open fractures, so water can be circulated through the rock and heated.

district-heating.short: Heating many buildings from one central source through a network of insulated hot-water pipes.

tidal-range.short: The height difference between high and low water. Barrages need large ranges, several metres or more.

tidal-barrage.short: A dam across an estuary or bay with sluices and turbines. It traps the tide and generates as water runs through the turbines across the height difference.

tidal-stream.short: An underwater turbine placed in a fast tidal current, working like a wind turbine in water.

ebb-generation.short: Running a tidal barrage's turbines as the basin empties towards a falling sea, after trapping water at high tide.

energy-period.short: The wave period that, in a sea of mixed waves, gives the same energy flux as a regular wave with that period. Used with significant wave height to size wave power.

wave-energy-flux.short: Power carried by waves across each metre of wave crest, in kilowatts per metre. Exposed Atlantic coasts often average several tens of kW/m.

oscillating-water-column.short: A wave device with an air chamber open to the sea below: waves push the trapped air back and forth through a turbine.
